channel.description: The Ark is the weekly newspaper of Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry

item.title: Belvedere eyeing drone rules before deliveries arrive
item.description: The draft ordinance would not touch flight paths, which fall under FAA authority. It targets where drones launch, land and drop off on the ground.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere is weighing a first-in-Marin ordinance to regulate the ground-level side of commercial drone delivery, preparing for a near future in which food and packages arrive by air.

City staff presented the council with a draft that focuses on how and where drones may take off, land and drop packages within city limits. The rules do not restrict overflight or flight paths, which remain under the jurisdiction of the Federal Aviation Administration. Instead, the ordinance targets the local, ground-level impacts of drone delivery that are increasingly drawing attention in the Bay Area.

In a report to the council, staff said the city’s narrow streets, constrained rights of way and limited emergency-access routes make it especially important to act before routine commercial drone delivery takes hold.

Mayor Sally Wilkinson, who helped staff write the ordinance, pressed for action.

“We want something on the books before this comes to life,” she said.

Other councilmembers urged caution. Councilmember Jane Cooper criticized the proposed language, saying it was too vague and could lead drone delivery companies to take advantage of it. Councilmember Pat Carapiet likewise worried that the ordinance lacked specifics in how it would be enforced and tracked. But City Attorney Andrew Shen said the vagueness was intentional, the city’s attempt to keep the law “flexible” as it learns to deal with a new technology and business practice.
item.dc:creator: The Ark
item.media:description: A Wing delivery drone lowers a package on a tether. Alphabet’s Wing announced in March that it plans to bring drone delivery to the Bay Area, and Belvedere is weighing an ordinance to regulate where such deliveries can land and drop off. (Wing Aviation LLC)

item.title: Strawberry Rec picks giant berry
item.description: The district wants public input on colors and design details before finalizing the playground, with GameTime presenting at Community Night Aug. 21.
item.content:encoded:
The recreation district will build a nearly 13,000-square-foot playground centered on a climbable 20-foot-tall berry with two green slides for arms and bouncy footbridges.

The board approved the design and hired playground company GameTime to build it for $2.4 million in a 4-0 vote July 14. Board member Sarah Waterfield was absent.

The district plans to break ground in 2027 on the play area, which it has called a “destination” and a “statement piece” meant to draw families to the recreation center off Belvedere Drive. It will replace Reggie Park, which the district removed in 2023 to make way for pickleball and basketball courts.

The district is also seeking public input. While it says it has decided on the overall design, the board wants feedback on the particulars: minor design elements, shapes and colors. The district will ask GameTime to appear at its annual Community Night event Aug. 21, where the company will present the design and take comments from residents.

item.media:description: A GameTime rendering shows the proposed playground in context, its climbable 20-foot strawberry and green tube slides set on a patch of grass between the district’s tennis and pickleball courts, foreground, and its baseball field, off Belvedere Drive. A barn play structure sits at left. (GameTime via Strawberry Recreation District)

item.title: Father chronicles daughter’s journey to the Paralympics
item.description: Marin Morrison was diagnosed with a brain tumor as a high school freshman in 2005. She qualified for the Paralympics before dying at age 18 in 2009.
item.content:encoded:
Marin Morrison’s passion for swimming was obvious the first time she entered a pool at age 6, says her father, Matt Morrison.

“It was clear right away that she was … extraordinary for a small child, and she just loved it,” Morrison says.

By the time she turned 13, Marin’s swim times were just 1.5 seconds slower than times that would qualify swimmers for the U.S. Olympic Trials. She even beat 17-year-old Amanda Weir in a 25-yard underwater race in 2003, Sports Illustrated reported in 2009, the year before Weir won two silver medals at the 2004 Athens Olympics.

Morrison says he expected his daughter to improve enough to meet those Olympic-level swimming standards by the time she turned 14, entering her freshman year of high school in the Atlanta suburbs.

“But that’s when … she was diagnosed, and the story became something very different,” he says.

Marin was diagnosed with a brain tumor during her freshman year of high school in 2005. She fought valiantly against the disease, her father says, qualifying for and participating in the 2008 Beijing Paralympics four months before she died at age 18.

Morrison, who grew up in Tiburon, chronicles his daughter’s journey in “Touched: The Marin Morrison Story.”
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Marin Morrison, daughter of Tiburon local Matt Morrison, qualified for the 2008 Beijing Paralympics in September following performances at the U.S. Paralympic Trials that August; she’s pictured at Beijing’s Water Cube, where swimming competitions were held. A promising youth swimmer, Marin Morrison set two national records in her para-swimming classification. She died of brain cancer in January 2009, aged 18. (via Matt Morrison)

item.title: Strawberry Rec rejects grand jury consolidation push
item.description: The district says its mission differs fundamentally from utility and safety agencies, since it runs mostly on user fees, not property taxes.
item.content:encoded:
The Strawberry Recreation District has rejected the core findings and most recommendations of a Marin civil grand jury report that urges the county’s more than 50 special districts to explore consolidation, arguing its role as a fee-supported recreation agency sets it apart from the essential-service providers the report targets.

The grand jury’s “Better Service at Lower Cost” report, released June 11, urges special districts to consolidate to increase efficiency and save taxpayer money. Districts must respond by Sept. 11. Strawberry’s board approved its response in a 4-0 vote July 14, with board member Sarah Waterfield absent.

Most of the report targets the county’s taxpayer-funded utility, infrastructure, emergency response and public safety services, calling for “deliberate, structured optimization.” Strawberry Recreation District says it is a special case. It funds most of its costs through user fees, not taxes, and its facilities and classes are open to the entire public, not just district residents.
item.dc:creator: The Ark

item.title: Beach Road seawall work is now underway in Belvedere
item.description: Drivers should expect single-lane traffic and sidewalk closures on Beach Road, with the sidewalk near the seawall closed via marked detour.
item.content:encoded:
Work tostabilize the Beach Road seawallis now underway, the start of a monthslong project engineers say is needed to keep the eroding wall from failing in a major earthquake and flooding hundreds of lagoon-area homes.

Pacific Gas and Electric Co. crews began relocating utilities in the roadway on July 17. That project is expected to run through July 29, with possible Saturday work July 25, before the main construction begins. Gordon N. Ball Construction Inc. of Walnut Creek is set to build from July 27 to Oct. 30 under a $3.51 million contract the City Council awarded in April. The work will install steel sheet piles reinforcing about 550 feet of seawall along Beach Road, between the Main Street and Peninsula Road intersections, part of a roughly $4.97 million project.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel
item.media:description: Tow-away no-parking signs line Beach Road, marking the zone where Pacific Gas and Electric Co. crews are relocating utilities ahead of the seawall stabilization project. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Belvedere’s new admin tech finds a career in public service
item.description: Jules Fogarty, 27, is Belvedere's new administrative technician, handling customer service, permitting, records and support for public meetings.
item.content:encoded:
Jules Fogarty’s first years in the workforce were defined by remote work. He graduated from the University of California at Berkeley in 2020, not too long after the pandemic hit, and spent his early career working from home as a data analyst and program manager for nonprofits.

So Fogarty, 27, says he’s happy to now be working at his first in-office job behind the front desk at Belvedere City Hall. He was hired as the city’s administrative technician in April; his responsibilities include customer service, accounts payable and receivable, records management, permitting and support for human resources and public meetings.

“I’m really liking it here,” Fogarty says. “The city’s beautiful, the staff’s really, really nice.”

He says he’s enjoyed getting to know residents and learning the ins and outs of the small community.

“In a bigger city or at the state level or federal level, it’d just be much harder to make relationships with the constituents that you’re serving at the end of the day,” he says.

item.media:description: Jules Fogarty was hired as the city of Belvedere’s administrative technician in April. He serves behind the front desk of City Hall, answering resident questions while also overseeing accounts payable and receivable, records management and permitting and providing support for human resources and public meetings. item.title: New Business: Hydration Room offers IV therapy, injections for health and wellness
item.description: Treatments range from a $215 hangover IV to a $65 Skinny Shot, plus ongoing GLP-1 weight-loss and testosterone-replacement injections.
item.content:encoded:
Hydration Room founder Dr. Brett Florie was a resident anesthesiologist at the University of Southern California when his wife began suffering from debilitating migraines. Drawing on his growing expertise in the field, he began experimenting with IV treatments for her.

“I put together a concoction intravenously, integrating Western and Eastern medicine, that had a tremendous impact on her life,” he said.

The experiment would later become the foundation for Hydration Room, the IV therapy clinic Florie started in Newport Beach in 2014, which has since expanded to 64 locations across California. The clinic opened itslatest locationat Strawberry Village June 12, taking over a vacant space in the center near Belvedere Drive. The location offers IV-injected vitamins, antioxidants, electrolytes and peptides, among other treatments. Hydration Room joins a slate of other health and wellness shops to come to Strawberry Village in recent years, including Orange­theory Fitness in 2018, Hot Yoga Republic in February 2025 and Club Pilates in June.

The Strawberry Village Hydration Room offers 37 IV and injection treatments with names like “Cold & Flu Remedy,” “Hangover,” “Jet Lag,” “Stress Rescue,” “Skinny Shot” and “Happy Shot.” It also offers ongoing medical injections like GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and testosterone-replacement therapy.
item.dc:creator: The Ark
item.media:description: Registered nurse Johana De Brauwere staffs Hydration Room’s new Strawberry Village clinic, where a row of recliners sits beneath wall-mounted IV bags. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A Pokémon Go player aims to catch ’em all in Tiburon
item.description: Tiburon landmarks like Town Hall and the Old Rail Trail double as in-game PokéStops, giving Cao a reason to explore the town on his lunch breaks.
item.content:encoded:
Denny Cao is tapping his phone screen on a lunch break from his job as a software engineer at Tiburon’s Digital Foundry.

But he’s not checking email or texting. The 29-year-old Fremont resident is trying to defeat an animated monster near the Edward Zelinsky ferry landing in downtown Tiburon.

Cao and two colleagues were playing Pokémon Go downtown on July 8. The augmented-reality game for iPhone and Android devices sends players to real-world landmarks to catch, train and battle the “pocket monsters,” the formal name for the media franchise now featuring 1,028 creatures — and counting. The franchise began with 151 monsters when the original games were released in February 1996 in Japan on the Nintendo Game Boy.

“It just gets you outdoors,” Cao says of the game, which he has played on and off since before its official release in July 2016, when he was a beta tester. He says he was especially grateful for the game during the stay-at-home orders in the early days of the coronavirus pandemic in 2020.

item.media:description: Fremont resident Denny Cao, a software engineer with Tiburon-based Digital Foundry, spent his July 8 lunch break walking around downtown Tiburon playing Pokémon Go, the mobile game that became a cultural phenomenon upon its release July 6, 2016. item.title: Garden Plot: Names of plants, animals trace back to explorers, naturalists
item.description: Institutions such as the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew and the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh financed many trips around the world to collect specimens that might do well in British gardens.
item.content:encoded:
Both plants and animals are named after people, often those who discovered them, those who played a role in bringing plants to the trade or those who are friends. The British, keen gardeners that they are, were quick to realize the potential of bringing foreign plants to their gardens. Institutions such as the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew and the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh financed many trips around the world to collect specimens that might do well in British gardens.

The Age of Discovery started in the early 1400s, followed by the Enlightenment from the late 1700s into the early 1800s. People became fascinated with finding what else was out there, and seagoing ships were capable of longer voyages. The crowns of Spain, Portugal, France, England and others had financial motivations to discover things like rubber, coffee, spices and other lucrative trade items. These voyages often included naturalists and gardeners who carefully packed barrels of specimens to be sent home for study and cultivation. These trips weren’t without risk, as plant explorers died in the pursuit of more and better plants; David Douglas, for instance, died young after a run-in with a bull while hunting plants in Hawaii.
item.dc:creator: Diane Lynch
item.media:description: Clarkia, a pink native wildflower named for William Clark of the Lewis and Clark expedition, blooms along some of Tiburon’s fire roads each spring. (Diane Lynch / For The Ark)

item.title: Tracy Ann Breuner Jaquier
item.description: Tracy Jaquier of Belvedere
item.content:encoded:
Tracy Ann Breuner Jaquier was born in Sacramento in July of 1961, but soon after her parents moved to Orinda, CA, where she attended Glorietta Elementary, Inland Valley Intermediate (now Orinda Intermediate) and Miramonte High School. She enjoyed doing musicals, singing in the choir, and playing volleyball. During those years she was imbued with a deep love of California’s Sierra Nevada mountains. She loved jeeping and camping with cousins and friends around Lake Tahoe and her summers at Bob Matthias Sierra Camp near King’s Canyon National Park. Her love of camping, shooting, fishing, and taking long hikes endured throughout her life. Tracy was also at home behind the wheel of a boat, especially when cruising the west shore of Lake Tahoe in her father’s woody, the Barbara C.

After receiving a BA in Economics at UCLA, Tracy enjoyed embodying her yuppie years (her generation invented yuppies!) in San Francisco. One of her first accomplishments was introducing Wang personal computers to the stodgy world of insurance while at Industrial Indemnity. From there she moved to commercial real estate, finding financial analysis of prospective deals a perfect fit for her talents. It wasn’t long until she caught the eye of a fellow commercial real estate colleague while running with the Hash House Harriers in the evenings after work in San Francisco. In 1987, she married Guy Jaquier.

Starting a family while living in the Oakland Hills, Tracy gave up the working world for the family world. In 1994, she, Guy, her son, Will, and her daughter, Carly, moved to the island of Belvedere and never left. Dear friends from Orinda, UCLA, and San Francisco stayed in the mix and new parent friends entered as well, while she and her husband remained active in groups like the Junior League of San Francisco, the Guardsmen, the San Francisco Yacht Club, the Town and Country Club, and the Bohemian Club while their children grew up and attended schools in Marin and San Francisco. Tracy was an avid supporter of the Smuin Ballet and its astounding talent.

Not only interested in sophisticated city happenings, Tracy hosted major camping events, which included challenges to see who could create the most elaborate dinners in the mountains, as well as theme nights and costumes. Beloved by the families involved, preparations and planning for the next summer’s event would start on this year’s adventure.

item.title: Crowded field forms for Tam district board; no council challengers so far
item.description: Candidates for the Nov. 3 election have until 5 p.m. Aug. 7 to file, with an extended deadline through Aug. 12 in races where an incumbent doesn't file.
item.content:encoded:
Candidate filing for the Nov. 3 election has drawn no challengers so far to the Tiburon and Belvedere council seats, but a crowded field is taking shape for the Tamalpais Union High School District board.

Six candidates have taken out nomination papers for three seats on the Tamalpais Union High School District board, the most contested race on peninsula ballots so far.

Elsewhere among the roughly 30 peninsula seats on the ballot, most incumbents face no opposition. In Tiburon, Councilmember Alice Fredericks, first elected in 2001, took out papers July 15 as she seeks a seventh term. The two other council seats, held by Jack Ryan and Jon Welner, had drawn no candidates by press deadline. Neither incumbent had taken out papers, and no challengers had emerged.

In Belvedere, Councilmember Peter Mark qualified for the November ballot July 16, having filed his candidacy papers July 14. Fellow Councilmember Jane Cooper took out papers July 13 but had not yet filed. Both were first elected in 2022 and seek second terms, their last under a local custom that limits members to two terms. No challengers had surfaced for the two seats.

Candidates must file by 5 p.m. Aug. 7. If any incumbent in a race does not file, challengers in that race may continue to file through 5 p.m. 12.

Interested residents may obtain nomination papers from Tiburon Town Clerk Lea Dilena at 415-435-7377 orldilena@townoftiburon.gov, and from Belvedere City Clerk Beth Haener at 415-435-8913 orclerk@cityofbelvedere.org.

Other peninsula races

Reed Union School District:Three seats and a $115 million school bond are on the ballot. Challenger Lina Godfrey, a Tiburon resident and disability-access advocate who serves on the town’s Diversity Inclusion Task Force, has taken out papers. Incumbent Mike Ghaffary, appointed to the board in February, filed his declaration of candidacy July 14. Board President Shelby Pasarell Tsai said she will run again but had not taken out papers. Board member Afsaneh Zolfaghari is not seeking reelection.

Tamalpais Union High School District:Six candidates have taken out papers for the three seats. The five challengers are Leslie Harlander, a former board member and 2020 board president; Brian Sutherland, a constitutional lawyer with two sons at Tamalpais High School, who filed July 16; Cynthia Joy Scully Koo, a Mill Valley resident who co-organizes the Marin Youth Job Fair; Maria Sandoval, a Mill Valley Spanish t...

item.title: Belvedere issues Mallard Pointe demolition permit, clearing way for evictions
item.description: Belvedere has issued the demolition permit for Mallard Pointe, letting the developer begin evicting tenants of the 22-unit lagoon complex.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere has issued the demolition permit forMallard Pointe, allowing the developer to start evicting residents of the 22-unit lagoon-side complex. But it can’t begin tearing down the duplexes until the city approves a separate bulkhead permit, which remains under review.

The city issued the permit July 15, advancing a six-year effort to replace the market-rate rental units between City Hall and Belvedere Lagoon with a 40-unit development. Developer Thompson Dorfman Partners LLC must now serve tenants at 1-22 Mallard Road with formal notices to vacate. Once those notices go out, residents will have 60 days to leave, putting move-out around mid-September.

Issuing the permit starts the eviction clock, but demolition still depends on the bulkhead permit. The developer will work to secure it during the 60-day notice period, the city said. If it cannot, tenants could be forced out before any teardown can legally begin, a scenario residents have warned about.

At aJuly 9 community meetingthat drew about 100 residents, Belvedere’s specialist housing attorney Barbara Kautz pointed to state building and housing law.

“If the conditions of approval have been met, the city is required to issue the demolition permit,” she said. If the city refused, she said, that would be evidence of bad faith under those laws, and “the city could be subject to pretty severe penalties.”

Mayor Sally Wilkinson echoed that view, saying councilmembers are “bound to follow the law” and have “fiduciary responsibilities to the city … in terms of our fiscal position and not exposing ourselves to unnecessary legal risk.”

What the permit means for tenants

Tenants received a 180-day notice to vacate dated Feb. 6 that said their tenancies were expected to end Aug. 5, according to a city FAQ posted July 15. That letter, required by state law and the project’s conditions of approval, could not force anyone out. A formal 60-day notice could be issued only after the demolition permit was granted.

The developer has said it will send the notices as soon as it has the permit in hand. After the 60-day period ends, Thompson Dorfman will have 75 days to complete demolition.

If a tenant does not leave after 60 days, the city said it would assess conditions and decide whether partial demolition could proceed in vacated areas, but only if the work could be done safely and within the permit. Under state law, a landlord may not try to force tenant...

item.title: Belvedere expects to issue Mallard Pointe demolition permit this week
item.description: About 100 residents packed Belvedere City Hall July 9 to raise concerns about the demolition, including fears over pollution, asbestos and displaced tenants.
item.content:encoded:
The developer behind the Mallard Pointe project has met about 95% of the conditions needed to obtain a demolition permit, with city staff saying they expect to issue that approval sometime this week. Demolition could begin as early as September — despite pushback from some 100 residents who packed City Hall at a July 9 community meeting to voice their continuing concerns about the project.

Just one of the conditions of approval for demolition was outstanding as of July 10 — the city was waiting for developer Thompson Dorfman Partners LLC to formally agree to begin replacing the lagoon bulkheads adjacent to the project within 14 days of starting demolition and to complete that work by Oct. 15.

Once the permit is issued, the developer must issue a 60-day eviction notice to current residents. After that 60-day period is up, Thompson Dorfman will have 75 days to complete demolition.

The issuance of the demolition permit will mark a major milestone in the six-year effort to redevelop the property, located at 1-22 Mallard Road. The project will replace 22 existing units between City Hall and Belvedere Lagoon with 40 units that are a mix of an apartment building, townhomes, duplexes and single-family homes. Four units must be set aside as affordable for low- and very-low-income households for 55 years.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Belvedere homeowners drawing lines on the Strip
item.description: Beach Road residents warned that disputing what counts as a structure on the Strip could open the city to a legal quagmire over land ownership.
item.content:encoded:
Beach Road homeowners are urging Belvedere to weigh legal risk and hillside stability before it changes how it regulates private structures on the Strip, the city-owned shoreline it has held since 1897.

Six residents turned out for the July 8 meeting of the Parks, Open Spaces and Lanes Committee, which the City Council has tasked with surveying what has been built on the Strip under revocable licenses. Their comments centered on two questions: what the 19th-century deed means by a “structure” and where the Strip’s boundaries lie.

The Strip is a corridor of city-owned land along Belvedere Cove, running from 172 Beach Road, near the Harry B. Allen public stairs, to 340 Beach Road. Belvedere Land Co. deeded it to the city in 1897 to be held in trust “as a general public beach or parkway and water front,” with language requiring that no structure impede “the free passage of pedestrians from one end to the other thereof.” The deed includes a reversion clause: if its conditions are violated, the land returns to the land company.

How much of the shoreline the Strip encompasses, and where it ends relative to the beach and the city’s adjacent tide lots, is among the questions the committee is working to pin down. Under city policy, the two are handled separately: dock leases govern structures over the water, while revocable licenses cover improvements on the Strip. Many Beach Road properties hold both.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Belvedere Island’s rocky shoreline at the base of the Harry B. Private docks, piers and a boathouse line the shore beyond. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Crime in Tiburon falls from 2024 spike; Belvedere ties record low
item.description: The declines mirror trends across Marin and California, where both violent and property crime rates fell again in 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Crime in Tiburon fell 26% in 2025 as 2024’s theft spike receded, while Belvedere matched its record low of nine total crimes, none violent, mirroring continued declines across California and Marin.

Tiburon recorded 75 violent and property crimes, the fourth-lowest total in 41 years of state data, according to California Department of Justice figures released July 1. The drop returns the town to the range of 2021-2023, when it set three consecutive record lows of 74, 72 and 69, and erases most of 2024’s jump to 102, an 11-year high driven by shoplifting and thefts from vehicles.

The 2025 total also sits below every pre-pandemic year; the town recorded 82 crimes in 2019 and averaged 85 a year from 2016 to 2019.

Belvedere’s nine crimes tied 2024 for the fewest in state records dating to 1985. The city has now gone two straight years without a violent crime and has recorded none in 14 of the past 18 years.

Tiburon police Chief Michelle Jean, responding by email through Capt. Jarrod Yee, said organized retail theft remained one of the department’s most significant property-crime trends in 2025 and credited the town’s revived detective position with advancing its biggest cases.

Belvedere police Chief Jason Wu said nothing changed in 2025 and credited a steady approach for the city’s low crime.

“We believe the trifecta of maintaining (a) low crime rate for Belvedere are high visibility patrols, being familiar with residents and the community and addressing the quality-of-life issues via our signature ‘no call is too small’ philosophy,” he said in an email.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Anonymous donor lifts bird-art proposal for Tiburon
item.description: Tiburon's Heritage and Arts Commission has sent the proposal to the town's parks commission, with the Town Council needed to give final approval.
item.content:encoded:
Arts commissioners have recommended metal sculptures of two birds in flight as Tiburon’s next public-art project after an anonymous donor pledged up to $68,225 to cover the total cost of installation.

The Heritage and Arts Commission voted unanimously at its June 30 meeting to send the proposal from Sausalito-based painter and sculptor Nicki Adani, titled “Bird’s Eye View,” to the Parks, Open Space and Trails Commission for its consideration. The parks board would have to back the plan before the Town Council ultimately signs off on the project.

The metal birds, with wingspans of 10 feet and 11½ feet, would be depicted in mid-flight and elevated 12-13 feet above the ground on support posts, according to the proposal. The birds’ feathers are open, allowing light to pass through, with the phrases “Be You” and “Fly Free” cut into them. The two birds in the proposal are abstracted birds of prey based on the red-tailed hawk, though Adani previously said final designs would be developed in coordination with the town.

The cost of the installation would range from $52,270 to $68,225 depending on whether it is temporary or permanent and the materials used. Commissioner Jaleh Etemad, who is working with Adani to bring the exhibit to town, said the donor “is going to pay fully for this project whether it is permanent or not.”

item.title: Marin civil grand jury urges mergers of Tiburon Peninsula special districts
item.description: The report points to fee gaps between Tiburon Peninsula sewer districts as one sign that consolidation could lower costs for ratepayers.
item.content:encoded:
Marin’s civil grand jury is urging consolidation among the more than 50 special districts that provide fire-protection, water, sanitation and refuse services across the county, saying doing so would increase efficiency and save taxpayer money. However, some local officials have expressed skepticism and say the complex issue needs to be approached with caution.

“The grand jury ultimately finds that the status quo is increasingly misaligned with Marin’s long-term needs,” the grand jury wrote in “Better Service at Lower Cost — Optimizing Essential Services for the Future of Marin,” released in June. “The time to begin deliberate, structured optimization of special districts is now.”

The report requires official responses from the special districts — including Sanitary District No. 5 of Marin County, the Richardson Bay Sanitary District, the Tiburon and Southern Marin fire protection districts and the Strawberry Recreation District — by Sept. 11.

Richardson Bay district manager Johnny Tucker expressed pause over the report’s findings, particularly given what he said was a history of previous attempts and failures, including failed votes to consolidate a group of sanitary districts more than a decade ago.

“Given this history, any future consolidation proposals should be carefully evaluated and supported by clear evidence demonstrating tangible benefits to ratepayers, including measurable cost savings, improved service levels or both,” Tucker said.

However, officials at some districts on the Tiburon Peninsula, including the Richardson Bay Sanitary District, headquartered on Tiburon Boulevard, expressed reservations about the report’s findings. item.content:encoded:
The Tiburon Peninsula Little League All-Stars closed out their District 3 tournament runs last week, with both the 10-and-under and 12-and-under teams finishing third in their divisions.

The 12U team, the club’s Little League division, ended at 5-3 overall. The 10U team finished 6-4.

Little League All-Stars

Tiburon carried a 5-1 record into the winners’ bracket semifinals but lost 3-1 to Mill Valley on July 8, dropping into the elimination bracket. Mill Valley scored both its runs in the first inning, one on a run-scoring double play. Ari Dodds started and allowed three runs, one earned, over 2⅔ innings, striking out two. Tiburon managed a hit each from Diego Sayle, Jackson Maunder and Henry Robinson and turned a double play.

A day later, Tiburon’s season ended with a 13-5 loss to Twin Cities on July 9. Tiburon trailed 4-0 before erupting for five runs on six hits in the third inning to take a 5-4 lead, capped by Cole Peters’ three-run home run on an 0-2 count. Twin Cities regained the lead in the bottom of the inning and put the game away with six runs in the fifth. Peters went 2-for-3 with three RBIs, and Tiburon finished with 10 hits. Luke Isaacson started on the mound.

Across the tournament, Dodds, Isaacson and William Dollard anchored the pitching staff, and Peters was steady behind the plate. Robinson and Troy Marsella held down the middle infield. Marsella also homered during pool play, joining Dodds and Peters with a home run in the run to the bracket.

Seeded No. 5, Tiburon won four straight elimination-bracket games before falling in the division’s final three.

The 10U team beat Ross Valley 6-5 on July 6, scoring the go-ahead run in the fifth inning. Mac Cabeal doubled home a run in the first, and Tiburon built a 4-1 lead through three before Ross Valley pulled even. Cabeal’s single knotted the game at five in the fourth. Cabeal went 3-for-4 with three RBIs, and Rex Davenport, Cabeal and Nick Morse each had three hits in a 12-hit game. Ryan Lambert started and struck out four over 2⅔ innings.

Tiburon beat Mill Valley 6-1 on July 7 at Boyle Park, breaking a 1-1 tie with five runs in the seventh inning on Cabeal’s three-run double. Cabeal went 2-for-3 with three RBIs. Thomas Osher allowed one run over four innings, and Davenport struck out two over three scoreless innings in relief.

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A waterfront walk at Blackie’s Pasture keeps three teens active
item.description: Trinity Winchester, Kate Rubel and Cole Norgaard are all smiles walking the shoreline path at Blackie's Pasture, a favorite spot to stay active.
item.content:encoded:
Trinity Winchester, Kate Rubel and Cole Norgaard fall into an easy rhythm walking along the shoreline path at Blackie’s Pasture on July 8.

For Trinity and Kate, both 17 and incoming seniors at Redwood High School, the walks are a way to stay active and frequently follow their early-morning gym sessions. For Cole, a recent Redwood High graduate, the walks are a chance to enjoy the scenery.

“We go on this walk a lot,” Trinity says, adding that she also takes advantage of the trails in Kentfield, where she lives. “Around here we go on lots of hikes, look at views. Up where I live, there’s also lots of trails like Phoenix Lake. … I go hiking a lot.”

item.title: Herbert Stanley Briggin
item.description: Long-term Belvedere resident Herbert “Herb” Briggin passed away peacefully at Drake Terrace, San Rafael, surrounded by family on June 26, 2026, at the age of 96.
item.content:encoded:
Long-term Belvedere resident Herbert “Herb” Briggin passed away peacefully at Drake Terrace, San Rafael, surrounded by family on June 26, 2026, at the age of 96.

Born on November 3, 1929, in New York City, Herb grew up in Larchmont, New York, with his younger sister, Barbara, and younger brother, Cliff. He graduated from Phillips Academy Andover and earned a Bachelor of Arts degree from Yale University.

During the Korean War, Herb enlisted in the U.S. Army and was selected for intelligence work. After studying Russian at the Army Language School in Monterey, California, he served at the National Security Agency in Washington, D.C., translating Russian during the early years of the Cold War. While in Washington, he and his first wife, Lorinda Knight, welcomed their daughter, Laura.

The family later moved to Southern California, where sons Stanley and Cliff were born. Herb built a successful career in broadcasting with Golden West Broadcasting, beginning in radio sales before advancing to management positions in Los Angeles, Seattle, and San Francisco. He later served as general manager of KSFO radio.

Herb’s second career was in sports marketing, where he worked with Matt Levine on projects for the Oakland A’s, San Francisco Giants, Golden State Warriors, and as part of the startup marketing team for the San Jose Sharks.

In 1989, Herb married Anne Schmitt, beginning a 37-year loving partnership filled with family, travel, and adventure. During their first year of retirement, they spent nine months traveling through Europe, ending with a three-month stint teaching marketing at the Estonian Business School in Tallinn.

Standing 6 feet, 5 inches tall, with his trademark bushy eyebrows, Herb was known for his intelligence, curiosity, kindness, wit, and generous spirit. He loved hiking, music, history, the ocean, and Marin County. He founded a men’s book club, enjoyed lively conversation, and had a gift for making people feel welcome.

Herb was preceded in death by his son Stanley and his sister Barbara. He is survived by his wife, Anne; his brother, Cliff (Irene); his children, Laura and Cliff (Nancy); his stepchildren, Amy Faulkner (Andrew), Eric Schmitt (Felice), and Will Schmitt (Heng-Jin); eight grandchildren; and one great-grandchild.
